second_reviewer_summary: SEM of how social capital shapes Iranian farmers' intention to cut groundwater use. It is water-conservation behaviour in an arid setting with no climate-adaptation framing and no adaptation action or outcome measured, so the concept criterion fails; the arid-water-scarcity context is only borderline.
population_rationale: Generic 'active farmers' irrigating crops in Kerman Province, Iran (upper-middle income); no commercial-scale focus and no smallholder label, so the generic-farmers rule applies. Evidence: "data were collected from 388 active farmers in the western region of the Jazmorian Wetland, located in Kerman Province (southern Iran)" [p.1, Abstract]
concept_rationale: Measures farmers' behavioural intention to reduce groundwater use (water-conservation behaviour change) plus water-management knowledge and ecological cognition, i.e. a decision/behaviour process under water scarcity. But it is intention only, not adoption of a practice, and is framed as sustainable resource management rather than adaptation. Evidence: "social capital in reducing groundwater consumption for agricultural irrigation in arid and semi-arid regions of Iran" [p.1, Abstract]
context_rationale: Agricultural irrigation under groundwater depletion and water scarcity in an arid/semi-arid basin; codebook accepts water scarcity or aridity in semi-arid regions as an implied climate link, although the text never frames the problem as climate change or drought. Evidence: "the basin is classified as arid to semiarid, with a long-term average annual rainfall of 170 mm over the past 40 years" [p.3, Study Area]
methodology_rationale: Structured survey of 388 farmers analysed with PLS-SEM. Evidence: "Employing a quantitative research design and a survey method, data were collected from 388 active farmers" [p.1, Abstract]
geography_rationale: Iran is upper-middle income. Evidence: "arid and semi-arid regions of Iran" [p.1, title]

lead_rationale: Both reviewers: positive-deviance technology adoption among peri-urban dairy farmers; climate background only. Also published January 2026.
second_reviewer_summary: Qualitative positive-deviance study of technology adoption by Ethiopian peri-urban dairy farmers. Climate is one background stressor among many (urbanisation, land loss), so the climate-context criterion is not clearly met, and the population is not established as smallholder; also published January 2026 (outside window).
exclusion_reason: Context criterion fails: climate is background only (not driving the research question); concept borderline (general technology adoption by positive-deviant dairy farmers).
population_rationale: Smallholder dairy farmers in urban and peri-urban Ethiopia (an LMIC); sample is explicitly smallholder dairy producers, though positive deviants run relatively larger/intensive farms. Evidence: "Smallholder dairy production, in particular, is an important income and livelihood source in East Africa" [p.2, Introduction]
concept_rationale: Documents adoption of dairy technologies and entrepreneurial behaviour (adoption processes), but these are framed as responses to general production challenges (disease, land loss, urbanisation, feed cost), not as climate adaptation; climate is mentioned in a few sentences only. Evidence: "The main objective of this study was, therefore, to document PD farmers’ entrepreneurial behavior supports the growth of dairy farming and the adoption of dairy practices and technologies" [p.2, Introduction]
context_rationale: Climate hazard is background only: one paragraph (Environmental factors) and one abstract clause mention drought and climate-exacerbated feed shortage; research question and interview guide are about technology adoption and positive deviance, not a climate hazard. Codebook: climate mentioned only as background is excluded. Evidence: "Environmental factors such as climate change, including increasing episodes of drought and low rainfall, have exacerbated feed shortages and caused reduced milk production in Ethiopia." [p.12, Results] | "Questions posed during the interviews focused on the adoption of dairy farming technologies." [p.3, Research design and data collection]
methodology_rationale: Empirical qualitative study: 33 semi-structured key-informant interviews, participant observation on 15 farms, thematic analysis. Evidence: "Participant observations were also conducted on 15 of the 33 dairy farms included in the study" [p.3, Research design and data collection]
geography_rationale: Ethiopia (low-income). Evidence: "The study area encompassed the urban and peri-urban areas of Addis Ababa and the Oromia administrative regions of Ethiopia." [p.2, Study area]
period_language_rationale: English; published 21 January 2026, outside the 2005-2025 protocol window (flagged), but not pre-2005. Evidence: "PUBLISHED  21 January 2026" [p.1]

lead_rationale: R2 include: drought-linked food and water insecurity with measured coping responses in a smallholder panel; vulnerability framing makes it marginal.
second_reviewer_summary: Smallholder household panel in Nicaragua linking drought and climate variability to food and water insecurity, with coping-response indices and resilience/adaptation implications. Concept is the only mildly contestable criterion (vulnerability framing), but coping responses are measured and the map is inclusive at the margin, so include.
exclusion_reason: Concept borderline: food and water insecurity drivers and coping indices under multiple hazards, with no adaptation practice tracked.
population_rationale: Smallholder coffee households (<10 manzanas) who also grow maize and beans in northern Nicaragua, an LMIC. Evidence: "To be included, households needed to have produced coffee in areas no larger than 10 manzanas (5.9 ha)" [p.5, 3.3 Study design]
concept_rationale: Paper analyses determinants of household food and water insecurity under drought and other hazards. It measures household coping responses (16 food, 13 water coping mechanisms, weighted into coping indices) and discusses diversification, but no adaptation practice or intervention is tracked; it leans toward a vulnerability/food-security assessment. Borderline under 'coping/adaptation responses measured' vs 'vulnerability only'. Evidence: "We identify pathways linking hazards to livelihood vulnerability and assess the relative importance of climate-related hazards." [p.1, Abstract] | "we calculated a water insecurity coping index analogous to that for food insecurity." [p.7, 3.6]
context_rationale: Agricultural setting with explicit climate hazard (2014-16 ENSO drought, rainfall variability measured with SPI) driving the research question, alongside other hazards. Evidence: "a strong El Niño (ENSO) event and associated drought (2014–16)" [p.4, 3.1 Study site] | "We focus on SPI for the rolling three-month time window (SPI-3)" [p.8, 3.8]
methodology_rationale: Empirical mixed methods: panel household survey, regressions, focus groups, CHIRPS rainfall analysis. Evidence: "The two surveys completed by each of these 311 households constitute the core longitudinal sample for our analysis." [p.6, 3.3]
geography_rationale: Nicaragua (upper-middle income under World Bank classification at the time; LMIC). Evidence: "We conducted this study in Nicaragua’s north central highlands" [p.4, 3.1 Study site]

population_rationale: Randomly sampled rural women crop farmers (registered with the ADP) in southern Nigeria, an LMIC; smallholder subsistence context. Evidence: "35 women crop farmers were randomly selected from each circle giving a total of 420 rural women crop farmers for the study." [p.4, Methodology]
concept_rationale: Beyond perceptions, the study measures the decision to adapt and implementation of adaptation strategies and models determinants of that decision (education, credit, cooperative membership, perception). This is an adaptation decision-making process, not perception alone, though the thrust is perception-led. Evidence: "Approximately 89% had taken the decision to adapt to climate change with 81% supporting their decision with action" [p.1, Abstract]
context_rationale: Crop farming with climate change as the driver of the research question; rainfall and temperature variation are the named stressors, though no specific hazard event is analysed. Borderline on specificity, accepted because climate change adaptation is the explicit focus. Evidence: "Developing economies like Nigeria whose rural populace depends on agriculture would have its agricultural production greatly impacted by climate change" [p.2, Introduction]
methodology_rationale: Structured survey of 420 women, binary logit regression, FGDs and in-depth interviews. Evidence: "Data were analysed using mean, percentages and Binary Logit regression." [p.1, Abstract]
geography_rationale: Nigeria (lower-middle income). Evidence: "This study was conducted in Southern Nigeria which covers three of the six geopolitical zones in the country." [p.4, Methodology]

population_rationale: Small-scale farmers (rice/orchard households, <1-2 ha; small-scale shrimp farmers) in Vietnam's Mekong Delta. Evidence: "Twenty smallscale shrimp farmers in Phong Dien commune (a coastal commune in Ca Mau Province) were selected to engage in T-learning" [p.9, Background] | "Owning relatively small lands of less than one hectare up to 2 hectares and using mostly family labor" [p.7]
concept_rationale: Documents adaptation processes (transformative learning, behaviour change, adoption of VACB and mangrove-shrimp polyculture) and outcomes (income, diversification, self-reliance/climate resilience). Evidence: "Improved land productivity and climate resilience of smallholder farmers (Cluster 5)." [p.14] | "Some tried to sustain the last piece of mangroves in their ponds while some others agreed to diversify their crops" [p.19]
context_rationale: Agricultural setting with explicit climate stressors (erratic rainfall, flooding, drought, salt-water intrusion, sea-level rise) driving the research. Evidence: "erratic rainfall, increased flooding, extended droughts and salt-water intrusion" [p.2, Introduction]
methodology_rationale: Empirical case studies with household survey (n=120), in-depth interviews, FGDs, field observations and pre/post workshop questionnaires; indicators with targets. Evidence: "surveys followed by in-depth interviews covering 120 farmers were conducted in four communes of Phong Dien District" [p.11]
geography_rationale: Vietnam (lower-middle-income). Evidence: "case studies in Vietnam’s Mekong delta" [p.1, title]

population_rationale: Smallholder farmers (household survey of 323 households) in rural kebeles of Humbo Woreda, Ethiopia. Evidence: "The key CSA practices adopted by smallholder farmers include agroforestry, soil and water conservation, and integrated soil fertility management." [p.1, Abstract]
concept_rationale: Measures adoption rates of CSA practices, determinants of adaptation strategy choice (multinomial logit) and perceived effects on income, productivity and food consumption. Evidence: "it examines the barriers and drivers of CSA adoption, assesses the perceived effectiveness of these practices in enhancing food security and resilience" [p.2, Introduction]
context_rationale: Semi-arid woreda with erratic rainfall and drought; climate trends (temperature, rainfall) analysed and CSA presented as response. Evidence: "This woreda, characterized by semi-arid conditions, erratic rainfall, and frequent droughts, has long struggled with declining agricultural productivity" [p.2, Introduction]
methodology_rationale: Mixed-methods: structured household survey, KIIs, FGDs, field observations, Mann-Kendall climate trends, AHP/Likert and multinomial logit. Evidence: "This study adopted a mixed-methods approach, integrating explanatory and descriptive research designs" [p.2, Research design]
geography_rationale: Ethiopia (low-income). Evidence: "Humbo Woreda, Wolaita Zone, Ethiopia" [p.1, Abstract]

population_rationale: Rice farmers with average 0.5 ha holdings, mostly rainfed, in Sumatra, Indonesia. Evidence: "With an average land area owned by farmers of 0.5 hectares" [p.5, Results 3.1]
concept_rationale: Although perception-heavy, the study also measures farmers' adaptive responses (adjusting planting season, fertiliser, pest control, irrigation, varieties) with frequencies and aims to inform adaptation policy; not perception alone. Evidence: "Adjusting the planting season, the use of chemical fertilizers, and controlling pests and diseases were the most dominant responses by farmers in dealing with SCE." [p.1, Abstract]
context_rationale: Flooding and drought drive the research question in a rice farming area. Evidence: "since 2011-2018 it has always experienced flooding during the peak of the wet season due to the overflowing of the Batang Kuantan river" [p.3, Study area]
methodology_rationale: Structured questionnaire survey of 297 farmers with descriptive, Friedman and ordinal regression analysis. Evidence: "a total of 297 farmers were selected purposively to be interviewed" [p.4, Data collection]
geography_rationale: Indonesia (upper-middle-income). Evidence: "Kuantan Singingi Regency, Riau Province, Indonesia" [p.1, Abstract]

lead_rationale: Both reviewers: residue-burning cleaner-production/mitigation framing; intention only; no climate hazard.
second_reviewer_summary: Adoption-intention study of residue management as a cleaner-production and pollution-reduction measure in Pakistan. It has no climate-hazard driver and the climate link is mitigation only, so concept and context are clearly not met.
exclusion_reason: Concept and context criteria fail: residue-burning cleaner-production/mitigation and pollution framing, no climate hazard or adaptation action measured (intention only).
population_rationale: Survey of 420 crop farmers (rice, wheat, cotton, sugarcane) in Punjab, Pakistan; generic farmers label in an LMIC, with >50% described as small farmers. Evidence: "More than 50% are therefore small farmers" [p.5, 4.1 Descriptive statistics]
concept_rationale: The behaviour studied is intention to adopt sustainable crop residue management instead of burning, framed as cleaner production, pollution/health risk and climate-change mitigation, not adaptation to climate risk; only intention (not adoption) is measured. Evidence: "residue burning emerges as a very serious threat for efforts towards climate change mitigation globally" [p.2, Introduction] | "this study concerns the adoption intention for sustainable residue management practices instead of real adoption behavior" [p.9, 5.1 Limitations]
context_rationale: The driving problem is air pollution, smog, health effects and soil degradation from residue burning; no climate hazard (drought, flood, rainfall variability) drives the research question. Climate is background only. Evidence: "The burning of crop residues has led to various environmental and socio-economic problems" [p.1, Introduction]
methodology_rationale: Cross-sectional household survey (n=420) analysed with structural equation modelling. Evidence: "A cross-sectional survey was conducted in order to interview selected farmers using a semi-structured questionnaire." [p.4, 3.2]
geography_rationale: Punjab, Pakistan (lower-middle-income). Evidence: "The study is conducted in the Punjab province." [p.3, 3.1]

lead_rationale: Both reviewers: landscape-change mapping; adaptation incidental and climate one driver among many.
second_reviewer_summary: Short symposium paper on participatory mapping of landscape change in North Sulawesi. Climate variability is one driver among many and adaptation (livelihood shifts, resilience remark) is incidental, not measured. Marginal; I lean exclude because climate does not drive the question.
exclusion_reason: Concept fails (landscape change study with no adaptation measured) and context weak (climate one driver among many).
population_rationale: Villagers in five North Sulawesi villages whose livelihoods rely on farming (coconut, nutmeg agroforestry), fishing and other work; rural subsistence-type communities in an LMIC. Evidence: "people on small islands mainly rely on farming or fishing for their daily needs" [p.7, 3.2]
concept_rationale: A landscape-change/drivers study; adaptation is not the object of measurement. Livelihood shifts after droughts and eruptions are mentioned anecdotally but no adaptation process or outcome is systematically assessed. Evidence: "The purpose of this study is to understand the various functions, processes, and complexities in a landscape contributing to poverty alleviation, livelihood improvement, and environmental services." [p.2, Introduction]
context_rationale: Climate variability and drought are named as drivers of change alongside volcanic hazards, migration and infrastructure, but climate does not drive the research question. Evidence: "Natural disasters and an unpredictable climate will remain the main drivers of change in this landscape." [p.4, 3.2]
methodology_rationale: PRA tools, FGDs, household questionnaires, participatory GIS mapping; empirical though thinly reported. Evidence: "We used Participatory Rural Assessments tools, consolidated questionnaires, formal and informal interviews of various stakeholders, GIS-based participatory mapping" [p.2, 2. Methods]
geography_rationale: North Sulawesi, Indonesia (upper-middle income). Evidence: "We studied five villages (Kinali, Laingpatehi, Mawali, Batu Putih Atas, and Tatelu) in the North Sulawesi Landscape." [p.2, 2. Methods]

lead_rationale: Both reviewers uncertain. Adaptation-explicit, climate-driven (GLOF) case documenting unintended (maladaptive) outcomes, which the protocol lists as an adaptation outcome; Andean farmers are one of several stakeholder groups. Include at the margin and flag.
second_reviewer_summary: Historical case study of unintended consequences of a GLOF adaptation project and the ensuing water conflict involving Andean farmers and others in Peru. It is adaptation-explicit and climate-driven, but smallholder producers are not the distinct population and agriculture is only part of the water use. Genuine borderline; the lead should decide, with a slight lean to include under inclusive mapping.
population_rationale: Stakeholders include rural subsistence farmers and irrigators of Cruz de Mayo/Llullán, but the analysis centres on multiple stakeholders (state, multinational energy firm, municipality, tourism); smallholders are not analysed as a distinct group. Evidence: "including rural subsistence farmers, urban residents, national park officials, tourism promoters, the state energy company Electroperú, and Duke Energy" [p.1 Abstract]
concept_rationale: Documents an adaptation intervention (drainage tunnel and floodgates against glacial lake outburst floods) and its governance and unintended outcomes. Evidence: "Climate change adaptation measures can generate long-term unintended consequences" [p.1 Abstract]
context_rationale: Climate-related hazard (glacial lake outburst floods, glacier retreat, water supply) drives the case; irrigation for agriculture is affected, though agriculture is not the central setting. Evidence: "once in place, it could be manipulated by various stakeholders" [p.5]
methodology_rationale: Empirical historical case study using archival documents, newspapers and interviews with residents. Evidence: "Interviews with participants conducted in 2009 indicate that the Committee for the Recovery of Lake Parón" [p.8]
geography_rationale: Peru. Evidence: "Lake Parón in Peru's Cordillera Blanca mountain range" [p.1 Abstract]
period_language_rationale: Published 2012, English. Evidence: "Journal of Historical Geography 38 (2012) 181-191" [p.1]

population_rationale: Subsistence/semi-subsistence iTaukei farming and fishing communities in Fiji (LMIC); smallholder focus is explicit. Evidence: "participatory rural appraisal (PRA) research in three iTaukei Fijian communities" [p.10, Methodology] | "enhancing the climate resilience of small-scale farmers in the Fiji" [p.4, Executive summary]
concept_rationale: Documents community strategies for responding to climate stressors, decision-making, information access and governance constraints on adaptation (processes). Evidence: "community strategies for responding to climate stressors, and (iv) challenges communities face in deriving services from the landscape and coping with climate stressors" [p.10, Methodology]
context_rationale: Climate stress (cyclone Winston, climatic variability, dry spells) on agricultural landscapes drives the research question. Evidence: "Rural Fijian communities and ecosystems are facing frontline impacts of a changing climate, as illustrated by Tropical Cyclone Winston in 2016." [p.4, Executive summary]
methodology_rationale: Empirical PRA (participatory mapping, transect walks, FGDs, key informant interviews) with qualitative analysis; literature reviews are additional components, not the sole method. Evidence: "We analysed the PRA data using qualitative data analysis techniques" [p.10, Methodology]
geography_rationale: Fiji (upper-middle-income) with stakeholder meetings in Tonga. Evidence: "field research undertaken in the Ba River catchment of northwest Viti Levu, Fiji" [p.4, Executive summary]
period_language_rationale: Published 30 September 2017; English. Evidence: "date published 30th September 2017" [p.1]

population_rationale: Smallholder (Dagaaba) farmers in Upper West Ghana; 80% of the population are smallholders and landholdings 0.6-2.4 ha. Evidence: "The region's current population is 702,110, and 80% are smallholder farmers" [p.3, Case study setting]
concept_rationale: Assesses a community seed bank intervention intended to build climate resilience: access, governance, participation, loan repayment, and why it failed (adaptation process/outcome). Evidence: "the project's objectives were to enhance climate change resilience, democratic access to seeds, food security, and traditional seed exchange practices." [p.3]
context_rationale: Drought-prone dryland farming; climate variability is the stated rationale for seed banks and is explicitly examined as a cause of failure. Evidence: "this paper examines these questions with data collected from drought-prone northern Ghana" [p.1, Abstract]
methodology_rationale: Empirical ethnography: 144 interviews, participant observation, PGIS, FGDs and programme records. Evidence: "The empirical research includes participant-observations; 144 in-depth interviews; participatory geospatial data analysis" [p.1, Abstract]
geography_rationale: Ghana, lower-middle-income. Evidence: "Ghana's Upper West Region constitutes the main geographical focus for this study" [p.3]

population_rationale: Resource-poor subsistence spate-irrigation farmers (fields under a hectare in highlands; subsistence level) in Eritrea. Evidence: "the resource-poor Wadi Laba farmers have established the principle of ''full farmers' participation''" [p.7] | "To transform the farmers beyond their current subsistence level, modernization of the Wadi Laba has been planned" [p.13, Concluding remarks]
concept_rationale: Documents farmers' own water management, collective action, governance and seasonal migration as coping/adaptation to flood and rainfall variability, with livelihood outcomes (food and fodder). The term adaptation is not used but actions align with adaptation objectives. Evidence: "the Wadi Laba farmers have used a number of indigenous water management practices to cope with the (re)construction and maintenance requirements" [p.1, Abstract]
context_rationale: Arid lowland agriculture dependent on highly unpredictable floods and erratic rainfall; hydro-climatic variability drives the research question (borderline: no climate-change framing). Evidence: "The only source of irrigation water in the Wadi Laba (ephemeral stream) spate irrigation system is the flood, which is highly unpredictable in occurrence and amount." [p.1, Abstract]
methodology_rationale: Empirical case study with farmer interviews, group discussions, field survey and flood discharge measurements; methods are only briefly described. Evidence: "the Wadi Laba farmers for their willingness to participate in the interviews and group discussions" [p.13, Acknowledgement] | "Discharge estimations were carried out of several small-medium, medium, medium-large and large-good category floods using a velocity-area method" [p.6]
geography_rationale: Eritrea, a low-income country. Evidence: "Eritrea is among the poorest countries with 53% of its population below the poverty line" [p.4]
period_language_rationale: Published 2005 (protocol window start), English. Evidence: "Irrig. and Drain. 54: 1-14 (2005)" [p.1]
